study.title: Isaiah 43 The God who redeems, witnesses, and corrects
study.overview: Isaiah 43 presents the Lord speaking to his people in a covenant tone: he is the Creator, the Redeemer, and the only true God. The chapter alternates promise, confrontation and restoration. First, God guarantees presence and deliverance to his people in the midst of judgment and exile. Then he summons Israel to stand a witness against idols, showing that only the Lord proclaims, saves and rules history. He then recalls the exodus and promises a new work of provision and return. Finally, he exposes the guilt of the people, stating that, despite infidelity, he himself offers forgiveness for his own sake and also justifies his discipline over Israel.

outline.title: God calls by name and gathers his people
outline.explanation: The Lord presents himself as Creator, Former, Savior and owner of Israel. The central promise is not the absence of difficulties, but the faithful presence of God in the waters and fire, an expression of protection in the midst of judgment and affliction. He redeems, gathers the scattered from all sides and states that this people exists for their glory.

outline.title: The Lord challenges idols and establishes his witnesses
outline.explanation: God summons the nations and their gods to prove knowledge and power, but only the Lord can proclaim the past and rule the future. Israel, even as a blind and deaf people, becomes a witness to the one God. The text insists that there is no other savior and that no one can thwart divine action.

outline.title: The new exodus and the new thing God will do
outline.explanation: The Redeemer of Israel announces the fall of the oppressors and recalls the open path at sea and the defeat of Egypt's military power. But the focus is not on the past: God promises to do something new, paving the way in the desert and offering water on dry land. The purpose is to feed the chosen people and lead them to praise.

outline.title: The guilt of Israel and the grace that forgives
outline.explanation: The Lord accuses the people of not invoking him and having tired him with his sins, showing that the crisis is not a lack of divine care, but human infidelity. Still, God declares that he erases transgressions because of himself and invites the people to judgment. The chapter ends by recalling the sinfulness of leadership and public discipline over Jacob and Israel.

study.context: The given notes relate the chapter to Babylonian exile and hope of return. There is also a recurring link with the exodus, especially in the contrast between the old liberation and the new restoration. The text not only depends on historical memory; it uses these events as a basis to affirm that the same God who has delivered in the past continues to act in favor of his people.
study.theology: The chapter teaches, first of all, the exclusive sovereignty of the Lord: he is the only God, without rival, and no one can prevent his action. Secondly, it reveals redemption as a divine initiative: the people belong to God because he calls it, redeems him and gathers him. Thirdly, it shows that salvation has a doxological purpose: the redeemed ones exist to declare the praise of the Lord. Fourthly, the text unites justice and mercy: God disciplines the sin of Israel, but also forgives for his own sake, that is, for fidelity to his name and to his character. Christian readings see here a horizon that points to the redemptive work in Christ, but in the chapter the immediate emphasis is on the Lord's fidelity to his people and on the exclusivity of his glory.

scholarViews.insight: The so-called "do fears" is based on creation and redemption: the Lord who formed Israel also rescued him and continues to recognize him as his people.
The word of comfort in the midst of discipline shows that God's goodness takes the occasion of human weakness and does not abandon his chosen people.
The promise to gather the scattereds of Israel is presented as an announcement of a blessed period in which God brings back Abraham's offspring from all over.

questions: How is the certainty that God calls by name changes the way we face suffering, fear and dispersion?
How should our lives as a people of God serve as a testimony against modern idols, which promise security and identity?
What does it mean, in practice, to live as a people formed to declare the praise of God, and not to promote themselves?
study.practice: Take the chapter to prayer by recognizing two things at the same time: your dependence on the grace of God and your responsibility to sin. Practice concrete confidence in the presence of the Lord in situations of "waters" and "fire" of the week, and examine whether his habits of worship, service and speaks really point to his glory. It is also appropriate to remember that biblical hope is not limited to escaping the difficulty, but to be gathered by God and led to worship him.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided make probable historical connections with Babylonian exile, with the exodus and, in a comment, with a possible assyrian campaign; the latter should not be treated as the certainty of the text. In Isaiah 43:10, there is interpretive variation in the notes as to who exactly is called "my servant." In Isaiah 43:28, Adam Clarke proposes textual amendment; this is an editorial hypothesis, not a sure given of the received verse.
